typeAssociationPolicy: All sixteen associations are editorial analogies to documented public work, not claims of a verified MBTI result. Never say the reader has the same personality as this person. No endorsement, similarity score, success prediction or hiring inference.

figures.name: Marie Curie
figures.title: Sustained inquiry
figures.biography: A Polish-born physicist and chemist whose research advanced the study of radioactivity. Curie received Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry.
figures.parallel: Her long research program offers a concrete image of patient, concept-led investigation.
figures.limit: Long-horizon thinking and deliberate follow-through are the connection; a scientific career does not establish someone’s private preferences.

figures.name: Albert Einstein
figures.title: Questions before conventions
figures.biography: A German-born theoretical physicist who developed relativity and contributed to quantum theory. His 1921 Nobel Prize recognized work including the photoelectric effect.
figures.parallel: His theoretical work offers a memorable analogy for questioning an accepted model and exploring another explanation.
figures.limit: The analogy concerns ideas and inquiry, not intelligence or evidence that the reader shares his abilities.

figures.name: Steve Jobs
figures.title: An idea made tangible
figures.biography: An American entrepreneur who co-founded Apple and founded NeXT, and played a major role in Pixar. He helped bring influential computers and consumer devices to market.
figures.parallel: Turning a product vision into coordinated execution gives this preference lens a concrete public-life example.
figures.limit: A product legacy is not evidence of a verified type; this analogy is not an endorsement of every management choice.

figures.name: Leonardo da Vinci
figures.title: Connecting distant ideas
figures.biography: An Italian Renaissance artist and investigator known for painting, engineering studies and notebooks exploring anatomy, nature and machines.
figures.parallel: His notebooks connect observation with many possible inventions, an inviting parallel for exploratory idea generation.
figures.limit: The connection is the breadth of questions, not a claim about his type or a measure of the reader’s creativity.

figures.name: Rabindranath Tagore
figures.title: Meaning given a form
figures.biography: A Bengali poet, composer and educator whose writing reshaped Bengali literature. He received the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature.
figures.parallel: The movement between personal meaning, artistic expression and education gives this lens a thoughtful narrative parallel.
figures.limit: A body of work can illustrate a theme without revealing the author’s private psychological preferences.

figures.name: William Shakespeare
figures.title: Many lives imagined
figures.biography: An English playwright, poet and actor whose tragedies, comedies and histories continue to be performed internationally. His work includes Hamlet and A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
figures.parallel: Inventing different human perspectives is a useful artistic analogy for attending to inner meaning and possibility.
figures.limit: Writing characters does not prove that their author shared any particular type; this is a literary parallel.

figures.name: Maya Angelou
figures.title: A voice that reaches people
figures.biography: An American poet, memoirist and performer best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. Her career also included teaching and public readings.
figures.parallel: Bringing personal experience into public storytelling offers a parallel for communicating meaning in ways that connect people.
figures.limit: This compares one visible aspect of her work, not her verified type, personal history or the reader’s influence.

figures.name: Robin Williams
figures.title: Possibility in the moment
figures.biography: An American actor and comedian known for improvisation and for dramatic and comic performances. He received an Academy Award for Good Will Hunting.
figures.parallel: His improvisation illustrates making unexpected connections and responding to an audience in the moment.
figures.limit: A stage performance is a crafted public role, not a reliable account of someone’s private personality.

figures.name: Katherine Johnson
figures.title: Care in the details
figures.biography: An American mathematician whose orbital calculations supported NASA’s early crewed spaceflight programs, including Mercury and Apollo.
figures.parallel: The careful checking of consequential calculations offers a concrete image of methodical follow-through.
figures.limit: This is a parallel about a work practice, not a claim that any type owns precision or mathematical ability.

figures.name: Florence Nightingale
figures.title: Care made dependable
figures.biography: An English nurse, statistician and reformer who helped establish professional nursing education and used evidence to argue for better care.
figures.parallel: Building dependable practices around everyday care makes an accessible parallel for attention to people and practical needs.
figures.limit: Her reforms involved many skills; care is not exclusive to a type and this association is editorial.

figures.name: Serena Williams
figures.title: Practice with purpose
figures.biography: An American tennis champion who won 23 major singles titles in the Open Era. Her career also included major doubles titles with her sister Venus.
figures.parallel: Sustained preparation and competitive execution offer a visible sporting analogy for organizing effort toward a clear objective.
figures.limit: Sporting results do not establish personality type or predict what the reader will achieve.

figures.name: Dolly Parton
figures.title: Creating something to share
figures.biography: An American singer-songwriter and entertainer whose work includes Jolene and I Will Always Love You. Her charitable foundation created the Imagination Library book-gifting program.
figures.parallel: A public career that combines audience connection and a practical community project offers a theme of bringing people together.
figures.limit: The program and performances are biographical facts; the preference association is an editorial analogy, not a verified assessment.

figures.name: Bruce Lee
figures.title: Learn through practice
figures.biography: A martial artist and actor whose career spanned Hong Kong and the United States. He developed the martial-arts approach known as Jeet Kune Do.
figures.parallel: Testing and adapting a physical practice provides a useful analogy for hands-on exploration and flexible technique.
figures.limit: This is about a documented craft; it does not imply shared fighting skill, temperament or a verified type.

figures.name: Frida Kahlo
figures.title: Experience made visible
figures.biography: A Mexican painter known for self-portraits that combine personal experience with imagery from Mexican culture and the natural world.
figures.parallel: Her visual work offers an artistic parallel for giving personal meaning a concrete, sensory form.
figures.limit: The reader does not inherit her biography; an artistic style cannot establish a private personality type.

figures.name: Muhammad Ali
figures.title: Responding in real time
figures.biography: An American boxer and Olympic gold medalist who became a multiple-time world heavyweight champion. His public presence extended well beyond the boxing ring.
figures.parallel: The timing and adaptation visible in a boxing match offer a concrete sporting analogy for responsive action.
figures.limit: This compares a public sporting practice, not personal beliefs, aggression, capability or verified type.

figures.name: Freddie Mercury
figures.title: Expression with presence
figures.biography: A singer and songwriter who became internationally known as Queen’s lead vocalist. His songs include Bohemian Rhapsody and We Are the Champions.
figures.parallel: His theatrical performances offer a memorable image of expressive presence and responding to a shared moment.
figures.limit: Stage presence is a performance skill; it is not proof of someone’s private preferences or the reader’s talent.
